title: Gilbert-Varshamov Bound
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: For every relative distance delta there exist binary codes with rate at least 1 minus the binary entropy of delta, up to lower-order terms.
short: Greedy coding ensures good codes exist.
long: Greedy coding ensures good codes exist. It is the best known general asymptotic existence bound for many parameters.
proof: Choose codewords greedily, excluding the union of Hamming balls around previously chosen words.
consequence: It guarantees codes with positive rate and positive relative distance.

title: Binary Hamming Codes Are Perfect
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The binary Hamming code of length 2^m-1 has minimum distance three and meets the Hamming bound with equality.
short: Every word lies within one bit of exactly one codeword.
long: Every word lies within one bit of exactly one codeword. Its parity-check matrix lists all nonzero binary vectors of length m as columns.
proof: Syndromes identify all single-bit errors uniquely, so radius-one balls partition the space.
consequence: It gives an early and elegant example of perfect codes.

title: Binary Golay Codes
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: There is a perfect binary code of length 23, dimension 12 and minimum distance 7, whose extension to length 24 has minimum distance 8.
short: A rare perfect code with more than trivial parameters.
long: A rare perfect code with more than trivial parameters. The extended Golay code is deeply connected to the Leech lattice and sporadic groups.
proof: Construct the code via a generator matrix or quadratic residue construction and verify its minimum distance.
consequence: It is one of the most important exceptional codes.

title: Binary Reflected Gray Code
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The reflected Gray code lists all n-bit words so that consecutive words differ in exactly one bit.
short: Flip one bit at a time to traverse all words.
long: Flip one bit at a time to traverse all words. The closed version also differs in one bit between the last and first word.
proof: Build the list recursively by prefixing 0 to the previous list and 1 to its reverse.
consequence: It reduces switching errors in analog-to-digital conversion.

title: Gale-Shapley Deferred Acceptance Algorithm
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The deferred acceptance algorithm always produces a stable matching in the stable marriage problem.
short: Proposals and rejections converge to a stable pairing.
long: Proposals and rejections converge to a stable pairing. The version with men proposing gives the men-optimal stable matching.
proof: Once a woman rejects a man she never accepts him later, so the process terminates; a blocking pair would have proposed and been rejected.
consequence: It is used in school choice and residency matching.

title: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: With at least three alternatives, no social welfare function satisfies unrestricted preferences, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and non-dictatorship simultaneously.
short: Fair aggregation of rankings is impossible under these rules.
long: Fair aggregation of rankings is impossible under these rules. The theorem applies to ordinal rankings rather than cardinal utilities.
proof: Track decisive coalitions and show the family of decisive sets must be an ultrafilter, hence a dictatorship.
consequence: It reshaped social choice theory.

title: Condorcet Paradox
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Individual transitive preferences can yield cyclical majority preferences.
short: Majority can be intransitive.
long: Majority can be intransitive. Three voters with cyclic orders produce the paradox.
proof: Give explicit rankings A>B>C, B>C>A, and C>A>B, then compare pairwise.
consequence: It motivates the study of voting rules beyond simple majority.

title: Gibbard-Satterthwaite Theorem
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Every deterministic voting rule with at least three possible outcomes that is not a dictatorship is manipulable by some voter.
short: Strategy-proofness forces dictatorship.
long: Strategy-proofness forces dictatorship. It assumes voters have arbitrary preferences over outcomes.
proof: Reduce to Arrow's theorem via the interpretation of pivotal voters.
consequence: It is a central impossibility result in mechanism design.

title: Bertrand's Ballot Theorem
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: If candidate A receives p votes and candidate B receives q votes with p greater than q, the probability that A is strictly ahead throughout counting is (p-q)/(p+q).
short: The final margin determines the chance of never falling behind.
long: The final margin determines the chance of never falling behind. The result assumes a uniformly random ordering of the votes.
proof: Use the reflection principle on lattice paths from (0,0) to (p,q).
consequence: It is a classic application of path counting.

title: Primitive Roots Modulo a Prime
subject: Number Theory
statement: The multiplicative group of nonzero residues modulo a prime is cyclic, so a primitive root exists.
short: All nonzero residues are powers of one generator.
long: All nonzero residues are powers of one generator. There are phi(p-1) primitive roots modulo p.
proof: A finite subgroup of the multiplicative group of a field is cyclic.
consequence: It simplifies discrete logarithms and modular exponentiation.

title: Euler's Criterion for Quadratic Residues Modulo a Prime
subject: Number Theory
statement: For an odd prime p and integer a not divisible by p, a raised to (p-1)/2 is congruent to the Legendre symbol of a modulo p.
short: A power test decides quadratic residuosity.
long: A power test decides quadratic residuosity. The result is 1 for residues and -1 for nonresidues.
proof: Use Fermat's little theorem and the fact that the multiplicative group is cyclic.
consequence: It is the standard computational test for quadratic residues.

title: Counting Quadratic Residues Modulo a Prime
subject: Number Theory
statement: Among the nonzero residues modulo an odd prime p, exactly (p-1)/2 are quadratic residues and (p-1)/2 are nonresidues.
short: Squaring is two-to-one on nonzero classes.
long: Squaring is two-to-one on nonzero classes. The residues are the squares of 1 through (p-1)/2.
proof: The kernel of the squaring map on the cyclic group has size two.
consequence: It is the starting point for Legendre symbol properties.

title: Carmichael Numbers Fool Fermat's Test
subject: Number Theory
statement: Composite integers called Carmichael numbers can satisfy a^(n-1) congruent to 1 modulo n for every a coprime to n; the smallest is 561.
short: The converse of Fermat's little theorem is false.
long: The converse of Fermat's little theorem is false. Korselt's criterion characterizes them as squarefree composite n with p-1 dividing n-1 for every prime p dividing n.
proof: Check Korselt's criterion for 561: 2, 10, and 16 all divide 560.
consequence: They motivate stronger primality tests.

title: Infinitely Many Solutions to Pell's Equation
subject: Number Theory
statement: For any nonsquare positive integer D, the equation x squared minus D times y squared equals one has infinitely many integer solutions.
short: Units of a quadratic order generate infinitely many solutions.
long: Units of a quadratic order generate infinitely many solutions. The fundamental solution generates all positive solutions by powers.
proof: Continued fractions of sqrt(D) produce a nontrivial unit, whose powers give infinitely many.
consequence: It links Diophantine equations with algebraic number theory.

title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem for Irrationals
subject: Number Theory
statement: For any real alpha and positive integer N there are integers p and q with 1 <= q <= N and the distance from q alpha to an integer less than 1/N.
short: Pigeonhole gives good rational approximations.
long: Pigeonhole gives good rational approximations. It follows by considering fractional parts of multiples of alpha.
proof: Divide [0,1) into N intervals and find two multiples in the same interval, then take their difference.
consequence: It is the starting point of Diophantine approximation.

title: Minkowski's Convex Body Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: A centrally symmetric convex body in R^n with volume greater than 2^n times the determinant of a lattice must contain a nonzero lattice point.
short: Large symmetric bodies cannot avoid lattice points.
long: Large symmetric bodies cannot avoid lattice points. It is a foundational result of geometry of numbers.
proof: Apply Blichfeldt's theorem to the half-scaled body and compare translated copies.
consequence: It proves existence of solutions to many Diophantine inequalities.

title: LLL Lattice Basis Reduction
subject: Number Theory
statement: The LLL algorithm finds a reduced lattice basis in polynomial time whose first vector is within a fixed exponential factor of the shortest lattice vector.
short: Gram-Schmidt and size reduction yield short vectors.
long: Gram-Schmidt and size reduction yield short vectors. It works in dimension n with polynomial dependence on the bit size of the input.
proof: Maintain the Lovasz condition on Gram-Schmidt lengths and swap or size-reduce until it holds.
consequence: It is used in cryptography, Diophantine approximation, and integer programming.

title: Zeckendorf Representation
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Every positive integer is uniquely a sum of nonconsecutive Fibonacci numbers.
short: Fibonacci numbers form a complete number system with no adjacent digits.
long: Fibonacci numbers form a complete number system with no adjacent digits. The greedy algorithm of subtracting the largest allowed Fibonacci number works.
proof: Existence follows by greedy choice; uniqueness follows because consecutive Fibonacci numbers are too close to substitute.
consequence: It gives Fibonacci coding and a curious alternative to binary.

title: Beatty's Partition Theorem
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: If r and s are positive irrational numbers with 1/r plus 1/s equal to one, the sequences of floors of nr and ns partition the positive integers.
short: Two complementary irrational slopes cover every integer once.
long: Two complementary irrational slopes cover every integer once. The golden ratio and its square give the classic example.
proof: Count terms up to N and show no integer can belong to both sequences, using the reciprocal condition.
consequence: It creates surprising partitions from irrational rotations.

title: Fibonacci Ratios Converge to the Golden Ratio
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers tends to the golden ratio, the positive root of x squared equals x plus one.
short: The recurrence settles into a fixed growth ratio.
long: The recurrence settles into a fixed growth ratio. Binet's closed form makes the limit immediate.
proof: Solve the characteristic equation of the Fibonacci recurrence and note the conjugate root has modulus below one.
consequence: It links recurrence sequences to continued fractions and aesthetics.

title: Sierpinski Triangle Dimension
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: The Sierpinski triangle is made of three scaled copies of itself by a factor one half, so its Hausdorff dimension is log 3 over log 2.
short: It is more than a curve but less than a region.
long: It is more than a curve but less than a region. Its area is zero while it has infinitely many boundary segments.
proof: Solve 3 times (1/2) to the dimension equals one for the self-similar pieces.
consequence: It is a canonical example of a fractal dimension.

title: Menger Sponge Has Zero Volume
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Iteratively removing the middle sub-cubes from a cube yields a fractal with zero volume but unbounded surface area.
short: Removing 20 of 27 sub-cubes each step kills volume.
long: Removing 20 of 27 sub-cubes each step kills volume. At each step the remaining volume is multiplied by 20/27.
proof: Compute volume and area scaling factors geometrically after k iterations.
consequence: It illustrates pathological behavior of fractals.

title: Tower of Hanoi Minimum Moves
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Moving n disks in the Tower of Hanoi requires exactly 2 to the n minus one moves.
short: Move the smaller stack twice and the largest disk once.
long: Move the smaller stack twice and the largest disk once. The standard recursive strategy is optimal.
proof: The largest disk must move once, requiring 2H_(n-1) moves of the smaller stack, giving the recurrence.
consequence: It is a classic example of exponential recursion.

title: Graham's Number
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Graham's number is an enormous integer that arose as an upper bound for a Ramsey-theoretic question about colourings of hypercube edges.
short: Its size is beyond ordinary scientific notation.
long: Its size is beyond ordinary scientific notation. Later work gave much smaller bounds, but the number remains a famous illustration of rapid growth.
proof: It is defined by a finite recursion using Knuth's up-arrow notation.
consequence: It popularizes the scale of Ramsey-theoretic bounds.

title: Goodstein's Theorem
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Every Goodstein sequence eventually reaches zero, although this cannot be proved in Peano arithmetic.
short: Organic-looking sequences terminate for ordinal reasons.
long: Organic-looking sequences terminate for ordinal reasons. The terms initially grow explosively before collapsing.
proof: Map each term to an ordinal below epsilon_0 that strictly decreases; Kirby and Paris showed unprovability in PA.
consequence: It is a concrete independence result for arithmetic.
